    14	# Parachute Resistance: Choose Parachute Size by the Speed Quality, Progress Over Weeks, and Use the Quick Release as a Contrast Method
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under the heading "Parachute Resistance Training" the authors describe small parachutes of different sizes attached to the trunk with a quick-release harness as "a low-inertia form of resistance" (Popov 1966). They note claims that the parachutes were developed secretly in Moscow in 1988 (Brunner & Tabachnik 1990) and say the Popov reference shows such research "more than 20 years earlier" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243). Their prescription (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244):
    17	- Drag "increases rapidly with velocity (actually the square of the velocity)." The drag force "characteristically varies between 5 - 200 Newtons for running speeds of 6 - 10 metres per second, depending on the size of the parachute (Zatsiorsky, 1995)."
    18	- Size by quality: "smaller parachutes are more suited for speed development, medium parachutes for speed-endurance and large parachutes for speed-strength and acceleration-strength." Since speed sets drag, the athlete should try "to run at maximum speed for as long as possible," using fartlek or interval methods.
    19	- Distances "commonly vary between 30m and 150m, with smaller parachutes being used for the longer distances."
    20	- Quick release at maximum velocity is "a special contrast method in enhancing speed and stride frequency" (also PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243, citing acceleration strength, 7.1).
    21	- Progression: "gradual progressive overloading ... with larger parachutes being used over a period of weeks," with periodic decreases in loading within a workout or microcycle, plus the sudden-release contrast method (see 1.16.3). Within a workout, "it is common to progress rapidly after the warm-up to the use of large resistance parachutes, then conclude with a few repetitions using smaller parachutes."
    22	- To avoid after-effects on normal skill, "precede and follow all parachute sessions with the same exercises performed without parachutes."
    23	- In preparatory weekly microcycles, sessions are "typically" two or three times a week on alternate days, and more frequent "nearer the later stage of the preparatory phase immediately preceding the competitive season."
    24	- Users can include distance runners, sprint or distance cyclists, and swimmers.
    25	
    26	The authors add that in the West the parachutes "generally have been applied fairly randomly with little knowledge of periodising them," and that "Appropriateness of use depends on an understanding of which strength qualities are required by the athlete at a given stage of training" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243).
    27	
    28	**Why it works** — The authors give the physics: the parachutes' aerodynamic resistance "increases rapidly with velocity (actually the square of the velocity)," which "allows us to use these devices more knowledgeably" and "Naturally, running speed determines the degree of drag resistance" (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244), so parachute size and running speed together set the load. Inference: velocity-squared drag is the textbook drag equation, and this relation is the only part of the entry that could rate `proven`; the size-to-quality mapping, distances, frequencies and progression are the authors' practice recommendations with no cited trial, so the entry as a whole is `supported`. The authors give no mechanism for why the quick-release contrast enhances stride frequency.
    29	
    30	**When to apply** — When adding resisted running for speed qualities: pick the parachute size for the quality targeted (small for speed, large for acceleration-strength), keep efforts near maximal speed, bracket the parachute runs with unresisted runs of the same drill, and place the sessions in the later preparatory phase. Eric's baseline: speed residuals drive programming: "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q16)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 97). Inference: the authors' "more frequently nearer the later stage of the preparatory phase" fits an off-season speed block that ends close to camp, but the book gives no in-season guidance for parachutes.
    31	
    32	**When NOT to apply** — The authors say parachute training "plays no role in the development of starting strength" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243), so it is not a starting-strength tool. They warn it can disrupt skill and correspondence (see [[claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence]]). The 5-200 N range is a secondary citation (Zatsiorsky 1995) without the parachute sizes that produce each value, so it cannot be used to choose a specific parachute. No frequency, distance or progression figure here comes from a reported controlled study.
    33	
    34	**Example** — The book's own: within a workout, progress quickly after the warm-up to a large parachute, then finish with a few runs on a smaller parachute, with unresisted runs of the same exercise before and after (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244).
    35	
    36	**Related** — [[claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence]], [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[framework--strength-speed-continuum-five-zones]], [[research-papers/petrakos-2016-resisted-sled-sprint-training-to-improve-sprint-performance-a-systematic-review]] (sled rather than parachute; the modern resisted-sprint evidence in the vault).

    14	# The Authors Warn That P = F x V Is Misapplied: Average or Peak Force Times Velocity Is Not Power When Force Varies; Use the Force-Time Curve, a Force Plate or High-Speed Video
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Scope of `proven`: only the identity P = dW/dt = F·v, which holds instant by instant for any force (Inference, see Why it works). Inference: the authors' statement that P = F.V needs constant force is imprecise and is not part of that scope; the claim that "many strength training texts" misuse the formula, and the advice on force plates and video, are the authors' judgment. The authors define power as P = dW/dt, "The rate of doing work at any instant," with work W = ∫F(t).ds, and note that "if F is constant over the interval concerned" this reduces to "the familiar basic expression for power": P = F.V, where V is the velocity of the object (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246; the equations are images, verified against the page image). In italics: "this basic definition is applied without qualification in many strength training texts and can lead to serious misunderstanding of training theory and methods." When force is not constant, one must use the general form (equation 4.1) and look at how force and velocity vary over time, "most conveniently" from F-V, F-t and V-t graphs. "It is inadequate to refer to average or peak force alone." In plyometric actions "the force changes very rapidly as a complicated transient spike function and cannot be regarded as a constant throughout the rebound phase," so "it is better to rely on a force plate or high speed video methods to analyse the movement than to attempt to apply elementary biomechanical calculations that will inevitably produce grave errors." (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246.)
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: with W = ∫F(t).ds, "if F is constant over the interval concerned," power reduces to "the familiar basic expression for power," P = F.V; "If the force is not constant over the time period being analysed, then we have to rely on a more precise form such as equation (4.1)" (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246). Scope of `proven`: only the identity P = dW/dt = F·v, which holds instant by instant for any force; the authors' constant-force condition is not part of it. Inference: because dW = F·ds, the rate of work is dW/dt = F·ds/dt = F·v at every instant, whatever the force history, so the instantaneous product F(t)·v(t) is exact. Constant force is needed only when one force value stands for a whole interval: then power over the interval equals that F times the average velocity. What fails for a time-varying force is multiplying an average or peak force by an average or peak velocity: the average of a product is not in general the product of the averages, and peak force and peak velocity need not occur at the same instant. That is the misuse the authors' warning ("It is inadequate to refer to average or peak force alone") actually targets. The practical judgment that "many strength training texts" misuse it is the authors' assessment, with no citations.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When reporting or comparing power or explosive strength: use instantaneous force-time and velocity-time data rather than one average force times one average velocity, and read the shape of the force-time curve, not just its peak or mean. For plyometric and rebound actions, measure on a force plate or with high-speed video. Eric's baseline: the force-plate reporting framework adds "'fluffy' metrics (peak power, average power, RFD) only with a specific, defensible rationale." Tagged **Adopted practice, framework not Eric's own** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 79). Inference: the authors' point gives one reason for that caution: single power numbers hide how force changed over the action.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Source oddities in the equations (verified against the page image, PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246): the text introduces equation (4.1), P = d/dt ∫F(t).ds, with "if F is constant over the interval concerned, we obtain," although (4.1) is the general form and the constant-force form is the one beside it, P = F.d/dt ∫ds; and the impulse is written F.Δt "where s is the displacement," though s does not appear in F.Δt. The authors' statement that P = F.V needs constant force is imprecise (see What it is); their practical warning against single average or peak values stands. The instruction to use force plates is general and gives no sampling rate or analysis method.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The book's own: a plyometric rebound, where force is a transient spike, so elementary average-force calculations "will inevitably produce grave errors" (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246).

Isometrics or quasi-isometrics can target the required angles (see 4.2.4), and "the selection of these exercises should be based on the joint angle at which maximal torque is developed in the special exercise" (PDF p. 256 / printed p. 245).
    17	
    18	The authors say that following these requirements "can sometimes lead to such initial positions using weights or pulley machines which are incongruous and artificial (Fig 4.22)," but add: "However, this occurs only when an exercise is attempted which fails to take into consideration the appropriate criteria" (PDF p. 256 / printed p. 245). Fig 4.22 (verified against the page image: one partner on the athlete's shoulders, another pulling the athlete's back leg, the athlete against wall bars) is a partner exercise in which, per the text, the partner on the shoulders "simulates the vertical loading which sprinting normally imposes" and the partner on the back leg offers resistance "intended to strengthen the power of the hip flexors." Its caption says the accentuated regions "can be incorrectly resisted and posture can be inappropriately held"; the text says it "may be appropriate if applied carefully," but incorrect positioning "can reduce its effectiveness markedly" (PDF p. 256 / printed p. 245).
    19	
    20	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is that the force peak of a sport action is tied to a joint angle, so training that peaks elsewhere in the range does not prepare that angle. They give no physiological mechanism here. Inference: this is the same angle-specific transfer question treated in Ch2 and 4.2.4 (see Related), applied to exercise choice.
    21	
    22	**When to apply** — Before choosing a special strength or isometric exercise: identify where in the sport action peak force occurs (early in a ballistic action, or at the switch between regimes), then set the starting position, range and resistance direction so the exercise peaks at that angle. Use isometric or quasi-isometric holds at that angle when the dynamic exercise cannot be positioned correctly. Eric's baseline: the isometric seated calf raise is run on ForceDecks at a "90-degree ankle/knee position." Tagged **Inferred (protocol)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 78). Inference: that is a fixed-angle test, not a training choice; by this criterion, an isometric training angle would be chosen from where the sport action peaks, which may not be 90 degrees.
    23	
    24	**When NOT to apply** — Source mismatch on Fig 4.21: the running text calls it "the graph of hip flexion torque in the air," while the caption reads "Change in the moment of the force during repetitive flexion-extension of the leg during the take-off for the triple jump" (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244). Inference: the take-off caption does not obviously describe a swing-leg hip flexion torque, so use the figure as an illustration of an early peak, not as hip-flexor data. The book's other sections qualify strict angle matching: isometric gains spread up to about 15 degrees either side of the training angle and further when the muscle trains lengthened (4.2.4), and Ch2 reports that training at a shortened angle transfers less across the range. Inference: training only at the accentuated angle may give less carryover to the rest of the range, so the criterion fits a supplementary exercise better than a whole program.
    25	
    26	**Example** — The book's own: sprinters' hip flexor work, where peak torque falls near the start of the leg's forward swing, so standing hip-flexor machines and loaded running miss it (PDF pp. 255-256 / printed pp. 244-245).
    27	
    28	**Related** — [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[heuristic--match-amplitude-direction-and-line-of-resistance-to-the-sport]], [[claim--isometric-regional-specificity-not-strictly-angular]] (4.2.4, regional rather than angular specificity), [[claim--joint-angle-specific-strength-training-narrows-transfer]] (Ch2, angle and transfer; qualifies this criterion), [[heuristic--isometric-priming-and-external-internal-classification]], [[claim--regime-switching-ability-decides-mixed-regime-events]] (the regime-switch instant this entry names).

    13	
    14	# Parachute Resistance: Choose Parachute Size by the Speed Quality, Progress Over Weeks, and Use the Quick Release as a Contrast Method
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under the heading "Parachute Resistance Training" the authors describe small parachutes of different sizes attached to the trunk with a quick-release harness as "a low-inertia form of resistance" (Popov 1966). They note claims that the parachutes were developed secretly in Moscow in 1988 (Brunner & Tabachnik 1990) and say the Popov reference shows such research "more than 20 years earlier" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243). Their prescription (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244):
    17	- Drag "increases rapidly with velocity (actually the square of the velocity)." The drag force "characteristically varies between 5 - 200 Newtons for running speeds of 6 - 10 metres per second, depending on the size of the parachute (Zatsiorsky, 1995)."
    18	- Size by quality: "smaller parachutes are more suited for speed development, medium parachutes for speed-endurance and large parachutes for speed-strength and acceleration-strength." Since speed sets drag, the athlete should try "to run at maximum speed for as long as possible," using fartlek or interval methods.
    19	- Distances "commonly vary between 30m and 150m, with smaller parachutes being used for the longer distances."
    20	- Quick release at maximum velocity is "a special contrast method in enhancing speed and stride frequency" (also PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243, citing acceleration strength, 7.1).
    21	- Progression: "gradual progressive overloading ... with larger parachutes being used over a period of weeks," with periodic decreases in loading within a workout or microcycle, plus the sudden-release contrast method (see 1.16.3). Within a workout, "it is common to progress rapidly after the warm-up to the use of large resistance parachutes, then conclude with a few repetitions using smaller parachutes."
    22	- To avoid after-effects on normal skill, "precede and follow all parachute sessions with the same exercises performed without parachutes."
    23	- In preparatory weekly microcycles, sessions are "typically" two or three times a week on alternate days, and more frequent "nearer the later stage of the preparatory phase immediately preceding the competitive season."
    24	- Users can include distance runners, sprint or distance cyclists, and swimmers.
    25	
    26	The authors add that in the West the parachutes "generally have been applied fairly randomly with little knowledge of periodising them," and that "Appropriateness of use depends on an understanding of which strength qualities are required by the athlete at a given stage of training" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243).
    27	
    28	**Why it works** — The authors give the physics: the parachutes' aerodynamic resistance "increases rapidly with velocity (actually the square of the velocity)," which "allows us to use these devices more knowledgeably" and "Naturally, running speed determines the degree of drag resistance" (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244), so parachute size and running speed together set the load. Inference: velocity-squared drag is the textbook drag equation, and this relation is the only part of the entry that could rate `proven`; the size-to-quality mapping, distances, frequencies and progression are the authors' practice recommendations with no cited trial, so the entry as a whole is `supported`. The authors give no mechanism for why the quick-release contrast enhances stride frequency.
    29	
    30	**When to apply** — When adding resisted running for speed qualities: pick the parachute size for the quality targeted (small for speed, large for acceleration-strength), keep efforts near maximal speed, bracket the parachute runs with unresisted runs of the same drill, and place the sessions in the later preparatory phase. Eric's baseline: speed residuals drive programming: "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q16)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 97). Inference: the authors' "more frequently nearer the later stage of the preparatory phase" fits an off-season speed block that ends close to camp, but the book gives no in-season guidance for parachutes.
    31	
    32	**When NOT to apply** — The authors say parachute training "plays no role in the development of starting strength" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243), so it is not a starting-strength tool. They warn it can disrupt skill and correspondence (see [[claim--parachute-resistance-tradeoffs-for-dynamic-correspondence]]). The 5-200 N range is a secondary citation (Zatsiorsky 1995) without the parachute sizes that produce each value, so it cannot be used to choose a specific parachute. No frequency, distance or progression figure here comes from a reported controlled study.
    33	
    34	**Example** — The book's own: within a workout, progress quickly after the warm-up to a large parachute, then finish with a few runs on a smaller parachute, with unresisted runs of the same exercise before and after (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244).

Consequently, the athletes referred to earlier who run with loads or use hip flexor machines regularly not 
only do not reproduce the required full amplitude of the movement, but also lose the ability to train the muscles 
to generate the necessary force at the appropriate hip joint angle. This clcarly illustrates the importance of the 
starting position for executing the special strength exercises that have a local effect on the motor system. The 
strength exercise should not only reproduce the full amplitude of the movement but also the specific direction of 
resistance to the pull of the muscles.
Following these requirements can sometimes lead to such initial positions using weights or pulley machines 
which are incongruous and artificial (Fig 4.22). However, this occurs only when an exercise is attempted which 
fails to take into consideration the appropriate criteria. In example illustrated, the partner seated on the athlete's 
shoulders simulates the vertical loading which sprinting normally imposes, while the partner pulling the back leg 
offers resistance intended to strengthen the power of the hip flexors. While this exercise may be appropriate if 
applied carefully, incorrect positioning or imposition of resistance can reduce its effectiveness markedly.
Flgirt 4.22 A special strength exercise intended to simulate the flexion-extension action of the hip during sports activities, where the 
Kccntuated regions o f force production can be incorrectly resisted and posture can be inappropriately held (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 
1999).
It is possible to develop force at the required joint angles with isometric exercises, because they can have a 
particular value in this respect (see 4.2.4). With isometrics or quasi-isometrics over a given range of movement 
one can locally influence certain muscle groups by paying particular attention to the accentuated regions of the 
movements where they arc involved. Therefore, the selection of these exercises should be based on the joint angle 
it which maximal torque is developed in the special exercise.
4.3.3 The Dynam ics of the Effort
The criterion of dynamic effort is the quantitative correspondence of the dynamics of the training means to the 
specific sports movement. This criterion states that the intensity of the training stimulus should not be less than 
that encountered in the given exercise at the corresponding level of sports proficiency and should even excced it. 
In other words, the effort exerted in training should not be less than the effort generated in the specific sports 
movement. One must now ask whether the maximum value or the mean value should be considered as the 
criterion of correspondence of strength.
Depending upon external conditions, a person can display maximal strength in two forms: in the movement 
ofheavy loads or light loads. The maximum force can actually be larger in the sccond case than in the first, since 
the lighter load can be rapidly accelerated (remembering that F = ma). However, it is unnecessary to exercise only 
with light loads, even if the maximum achieved corresponds closely to the dynamics of the special exercise. It is 
important to consider first the duration and character of the effort.
The fact is that the external force displayed in these two cases is qualitatively different: in the first, 
maximum force is determined by the absolute strength of the muscles, and in the sccond by the speed o f 
contraction. Therefore, the strength and training effects of the respective movements are also different.
From this it follows that, in striving to generate maximal effort in training, the athlete should become clearly 
acquainted with the type of strength which is needed and satisfy the criteria of correspondence according to the 
imount of effort and the movement time for the specific exercise. In other words, correspondence with respect to 
the maximum and mean magnitude of strength can be determined only by calculating the speed of movement. If 
the athlete finds the means for achieving this, he can be confident that he is on the right track in organising his 
special strength training.

2 4 6
The following examples serve to clarify the issue. If the special exercise requires the athlete to overcome I 
large resistance at a relatively low speed, then training should be aimed primarily at developing maximal strength. 
Conversely, if the athlete has to deal with a small resistance in the special exercise and execute the movement u 
maximal speed, then, according to the criterion of correspondence, he should apply a moderate amount of effort 
and pay particular attention to the duration of the movement.
4.3.4 The Rate and Tim e of Force Production
The criterion of correspondence regarding the rate of developing maximum force (see 2.2.1) complements the 
criterion of dynamic effort and is particularly important in those sporting activities requiring explosive strength. 
We have already stated that the strength displayed in training should be examined by taking into account its rate 
of production, which is equivalent to measuring the time taken to execute the movement. The production of 
explosive strength implicates a brief-acting moderate force whose characteristics may be described in terms of 
features such as the power and the impulse (F. Al) of the force, where s is the displacement and At is the brief 
time interval over which the force F acts (sec 5.1). The following factors are relevant in this context:
Here W refers to the work and may be defined in its integral form asW - jF(t).ds where s is the displacement 
produced by the force F. Thus, if F is constant over the interval concerned, we obtain:
The right hand side of this equation quite simply reduces to the familiar basic expression for power 
Power 
P = F.V 
.....where V is the velocity of the object
Unfortunately, this basic definition is applied without qualification in many strength training texts and can lead to I 
serious misunderstanding o f training theory and methods. If the force is not constant over the time period being I 
analysed, then we have to rely on a more precise form such as equation (4.1) which reminds us to consider how 
the force and velocity (as functions of time) vary over the time interval concerned. This can be done most 
conveniently by examining graphs of F versus V (e.g. Figs 3.15 - 3.18), F versus time and V versus time (e.g. Figs 
2.13,3.3, 3.4,3.14, 3.27,4.7).
It is especially important to be aware o f how the force-time (i.e. the RFD or Rate of Force Development) 
curve changes with time (i.e., the slope of the F-t curve, shown in Fig 2.13). It is inadequate to refer to average or 
peak force alone. The ability to increase power or explosive strength also depends on specifically training the RFD I 
factor (which was introduced in 2.2.1 as the factor that best defines explosive strength). This conclusion is vital 
to the design of strength training programmes to improve performance in any sport which involves explosive I 
actions. The emergence of plyometric training as an adjunct method of special strength training is one of the 
practical consequences of understanding the implications of the preceding analysis of power as a motor ability.
In all plyometric actions, the force changes very rapidly as a complicated transient spike function and cannot 
be regarded as a constant throughout the rebound phase. In such cases it is better to rely on a force plate or high 
speed video methods to analyse the movement than to attempt to apply elementary biomechanical calculations 
that will inevitably produce grave errors.
The other factor used to analyse explosive strength, the Reactivity Coefficient, was defined earlier (2.2.1) as the 
RFD relative to one's bodyweight (or the weight of any object being moved rapidly):
Reactivity Coefficient 
RC = Fmax/ tmax.mg = RFDmax^W
where Fmax is the maximum force exerted, tmax is the time taken to reach this maximum, the mass is m and g is the 
acceleration due to gravity = 9.8m/s2.
The above equations may be used to evaluate explosive strength, although the significance of each of them can 
be different, depending on conditions. Thus, evaluation using calculations of the impulse of the force is acceptable 
only when it is not necessary to compare different movements. If such a need arises, then the evaluation is valid 
only if the time taken is identical for each movement, a situation that does not occur in human movement. 
Therefore, in this particular case, determination of the impulse of the force is irrelevant.

# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's

    14	# Parachutes Avoid Extra Vertical Loading, but Resist the Flight Phase and Alter Landing Positions, Reducing Dynamic Correspondence
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors give one advantage and several limits of parachute resistance.
    17	- Advantage: parachutes "offer a safer alternative to the use of weights added to the extremities or body, or dragged behind the athlete (e.g. a car tyre or sled), because they do not increase the vertical reaction forces acting on the body" (PDF pp. 254-255 / printed pp. 243-244).
    18	- Limit 1: "parachutes offer the same degree of resistance during both the support and non-support phases of running, thereby disrupting speed and acceleration of limb and body movement during flight."
    19	- Limit 2: "parachutes alter the relative position of the joints during landing, especially during hurdling and jumping."
    20	- Together: "All of this can adversely affect several aspects of the degree of dynamic correspondence of the training means to the actual sporting movements (as discussed throughout Ch 4.3)." (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244.)
    21	- Scope: parachute training "plays no role in the development of starting strength, which is produced under isometric conditions" (PDF p. 254 / printed p. 243).
    22	
    23	**Why it works** — The authors' stated reasons are mechanical: no added mass means no extra vertical reaction force, while a drag force acting through the whole stride also acts in flight, where the sport has no external resistance. They give no data on injury rates for parachutes against sleds or limb weights. Inference: the safety claim rests on the vertical-force argument alone.
    24	
    25	**When to apply** — When choosing between parachute, sled and worn-weight resistance: if vertical loading is the concern, the authors' argument favours the parachute (Inference: for example, heavy athletes or athletes returning from lower-limb injury; the book names no population); if preserving flight-phase and landing mechanics is the concern (the book names hurdlers and jumpers), it counts against it. Eric's baseline: Dynamic Correspondence governs "whether an exercise actually transfers." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 103). Inference: a coach weighing a parachute block can use these two limits as the checklist for what to watch on film.
    26	
    27	**When NOT to apply** — The safety advantage is asserted, not measured, in the text; the book cites no comparison of injury or tissue loading. The sled is named only in the safety sentence, and the book does not compare sled and parachute on dynamic correspondence. Inference: modern sled studies (see Related) address performance, not this book's safety claim, so they neither confirm nor refute it.
    28	
    29	**Example** — The book's own: hurdlers and jumpers whose joint positions at landing are altered by the parachute (PDF p. 255 / printed p. 244).

    31	**Related** — [[heuristic--parachute-resistance-sizing-progression-and-contrast-release]], [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[heuristic--match-amplitude-direction-and-line-of-resistance-to-the-sport]] (the weighted-belt example: vertical loading trains anti-gravity muscles), [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--wearable-resistance-kinetic-energy-sprint]] (limb-worn resistance, which the authors call less safe), [[research-papers/petrakos-2016-resisted-sled-sprint-training-to-improve-sprint-performance-a-systematic-review]].

    13	
    14	# The Same Exercise Serves Different Sports Only If Its Regime Changes: Load, Tempo, Sets and Repetitions Must Match the Sport's Work
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The fifth correspondence criterion "relies on determining the character of the muscular work involved," and the regime "should be taken into consideration for selecting the means and methods of special strength training," because "depending upon the character of its execution, the same means can solve different tasks." The authors' example: "boxers and shot putters need to execute the same exercise (e.g. performing a thrusting arm movement against the resistance of a pulley machine) with different weights, tempos, number of sets and repetitions, because boxing requires primarily a quick, unresisted movement and the ability to repeat it many times without significant decrease in force, whereas shotputting involves rapid single movements against a specific resistance." The problem has two tasks: "selection of the regime for a specific motor action (e.g. the key elements in an exercise)" and "selection of the main regime which will best develop all of the diverse muscular activities in all-round training"; the second "is still far from being resolved." (PDF p. 258 / printed p. 247.)
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is that the training effect is set by how an exercise is executed, not by the exercise's name or shape, so the regime parameters must reproduce the sport's demand (repeated fast unresisted actions for the boxer, single fast actions against a set resistance for the shot putter). They give no further mechanism.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — After an exercise passes the movement criteria (amplitude, direction, accentuated region), set its loading parameters from the sport's regime: repeated low-resistance fast actions call for light loads, fast tempo and many repetitions; single fast actions against a set resistance call for heavier loads and few repetitions (Inference: with full recovery between efforts; the book does not state rest). Eric's baseline: "Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of 'sport specific.'" Tagged **Inferred (transcript + slides)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102). Inference: this criterion adds that position on that spectrum depends on how an exercise is loaded, not only which exercise it is.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The book gives the boxer and shot putter contrast without numbers, so it does not prescribe specific loads. For all-round sports (decathlon, gymnastics, modern pentathlon) the authors say the choice of a main regime is unresolved (see [[claim--all-round-athletes-main-regime-cyclic-and-phasic-tonic]]). Regime matching does not replace the other four criteria.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The book's own: a pulley-machine thrusting arm movement done by a boxer (light, fast, many repetitions) and by a shot putter (heavier, single fast efforts) (PDF p. 258 / printed p. 247).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[claim--regime-switching-ability-decides-mixed-regime-events]], [[claim--all-round-athletes-main-regime-cyclic-and-phasic-tonic]], [[framework--eight-types-of-muscular-tension]], [[heuristic--choice-of-muscle-training-regime-favor-combination]] (4.2, choice among isometric, eccentric and other regimes), [[elite-sports-performance--evans/case-study--dynamic-correspondence-applied-to-wrestling-takedown]] (Evans applies the regime criterion to a wrestling takedown).

    12	---
    13	
    14	# High Jumpers (Nikitin 1983): As Qualification Rises, Isometric Knee-Extension Power Moves Up and Plantarflexor Power Moves Down the Factor Structure
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors present factor analysis as a way to study the structure of special physical preparedness, "especially informative" when it compares athletes of different qualification or one athlete at different stages; data from many sports show "distinct changes in the structure of an athlete's physical preparedness with increasing sports proficiency" (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252). Table 4.1 (Nikitin 1983), "The factor structure (in %) of Special Physical Preparedness of high jumpers, in terms of the major factors displayed by a large sample of competitors of different levels of qualification," verified against the page image:
    17	
    18	| Factor | Class 2-3 athletes | % | Class 1 - MS | % |
    19	|---|---|---|---|---|
    20	| I | General athletic preparedness | 29.6 | Specific athletic preparedness | 27.4 |
    21	| II | Power of plantarflexors | 19.6 | Power of knee extension isometrically | 23.4 |
    22	| III | Power of knee extension in dynamic regime | 13.0 | Power of knee extension dynamically | 18.5 |
    23	| IV | Isometric strength of knee extensors | 10.5 | Power of plantarflexors | 11.8 |
    24	| V | Explosive-strength of knee extensors (isometric) | 6.5 | (none listed) | |
    25	
    26	The authors' reading: higher-class jumpers develop the specific ability to generate powerful take-off force (factor I) and powerful body extension with the knee and back extensors (factor III); explosive force of the take-off leg's extensors under isometric conditions (factor II) "assumes major significance," growing from what were factors IV and V in Class 2-3; plantarflexor indicators move from factor II to factor IV, "the contribution of which diminishes significantly"; and "the role of special physical preparedness of jumpers increases with level of qualification." (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252.)
    27	
    28	**Why it works** — Here the authors do give a mechanism. Isometric strength matters at high level "due to the large loading of the muscles during the take-off, where the support (take-off) leg acts as a lever, and converts into vertical lift the angular velocity acquired during the run-up." Plantarflexors fade "because under intense overloading the muscles of the support leg are already unable to make a significant contribution to the dynamics of the take-off." (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252.)
    29	
    30	**When to apply** — For jumpers and athletes whose key action is a planted, high-load take-off: as qualification rises, give more weight to isometric and explosive-isometric knee-extensor strength in the take-off position. Inference: the falling plantarflexor share may justify a smaller plantarflexor emphasis, but the book reports a factor share, not a training reduction. More generally, the authors' rule is to plan from "the general trends of change in the factor structure ... with increase in proficiency, as well as the individual peculiarities of a specific athlete" (PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253). Eric's baseline: isometric mid-thigh pull peak force enters the DSI used to choose between plyometric and max-strength emphasis. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 76). Inference: these data are a reason to keep an isometric knee-extension measure for jumpers, but they say nothing about the DSI ratio itself.
    31	
    32	**When NOT to apply** — The sample is described only as "a large sample"; the number, factor-extraction method and test battery are not given. The percentages do not sum to 100 (about 79% for Class 2-3 and 81% for Class 1-MS), and the text does not say what the remainder is. The labels changing between columns ("general" to "specific" athletic preparedness) mean factors are not the same variables across groups, so the shifts are interpretive. This is high-jump data; Inference: transfer to other take-off actions (a cut, a block) is not shown.
    33	
    34	**Example** — The book's own: Table 4.1 above.
    35	
    36	**Related** — [[case-study--skater-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[framework--four-level-functional-specialisation-and-special-physical-preparedness]], [[framework--isometric-contraction-categorization-voluntary-reflexive]] (4.2.4, explosive isometrics, which the text cross-references), [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]] (Ch2.2.4; agreement on qualification-dependent order), [[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/heuristic--correlation-methodology-limits-and-tie-in-effect]] (limits of correlation-based structure studies).

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Skaters (Shchirkovyets and Rosovtsyev 1977): Aerobic Factors Dominate at Class 1, Energetic Efficiency and Technique Dominate at Master of Sport
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Table 4.2 (Shchirkovyets & Rosovtsyev 1977), "The factor structure (in %) of special fitness of skaters in terms of the major factors displayed by a large sample of competitors of different levels of qualification," verified against the page image (PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253):
    17	
    18	| Factor | Class 1 athletes | % | Master of Sport | % |
    19	|---|---|---|---|---|
    20	| I | Aerobic power | 35.9 | Energetic efficiency of executing specific work | 36.5 |
    21	| II | Aerobic capacity | 23.3 | Multi-faceted technical preparedness | 21.9 |
    22	| III | Power of anaerobic processes | 16.8 | Power of anaerobic processes | 19.8 |
    23	| IV | Energetic efficiency of executing specific work | 2.7 | Aerobic efficiency | 10.9 |
    24	| V | Multi-faceted technical preparedness | 8.9 | (none listed) | |
    25	
    26	The authors note "the sharp rise in the role of energetic efficiency of special work and multifaceted technical preparedness"; that Class 1's first two factors "may be combined as one factor (i.e. aerobic efficiency) whose role at Master of Sport level decreases"; and that "the significance of anaerobic power increases slightly (factor III)" (PDF pp. 263-264 / printed pp. 252-253). Their conclusion: "a high level of aerobic potential still does not ensure top-level performance in skating. To efficiently generate a high level of aerobic power, it [is] necessary to have excellent movement technique and a high level of anaerobic (non-oxidative glycolytic) productivity." Factor research gives "a useful statistical model" of special physical preparedness, whose form depends on the individual's motor qualities and the organisation of training, so programming must consider general trends with rising proficiency, individual peculiarities and changes in the main functional characteristics (PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253).
    27	
    28	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism beyond the statement that technique and anaerobic productivity are needed to use aerobic power efficiently.
    29	
    30	**When to apply** — When an athlete's aerobic markers are already high but performance stalls: shift emphasis toward economy of the specific work, technical preparedness and anaerobic power, as the Master of Sport structure suggests. Eric's baseline: "Movement efficiency (skill) is treated as directly reducing energy cost." Tagged **Inferred (transcript)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 172). Inference: the rise of "energetic efficiency of executing specific work" to the first factor at Master of Sport level (36.5%) is consistent with that teaching point; the Class 1 value for the same factor (2.7) is unclear, so the size of the change should not be quoted.
    31	
    32	**When NOT to apply** — The sample is "a large sample" with no number, method or test battery given. The columns do not sum to 100 (about 88% and 89%), and the remainder is not explained. Factor labels differ between columns, so the comparison is interpretive. Class 1 factor IV (2.7) is smaller than factor V (8.9), against the order of factors by share (verified against the page image, PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253). Inference: 2.7 may be a misprint (12.7 would restore the order and bring the column to about 98%: 35.9 + 23.3 + 16.8 + 12.7 + 8.9 = 97.6), but the source gives no correction, so treat the 2.7 value as unclear. The conclusion that a "high level of anaerobic (non-oxidative glycolytic) productivity" is necessary conflicts with the authors' earlier advice in 4.4 to "decrease the proportion of glycolysis" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249); see [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]].
    33	
    34	**Example** — The book's own: Table 4.2 above.
    35	
    36	**Related** — [[case-study--high-jumper-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[claim--vo2max-alone-does-not-determine-endurance-performance]], [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]], [[framework--four-level-functional-specialisation-and-special-physical-preparedness]], [[claim--exercise-economy-improves-with-skill-and-interval-style-costs-more]] (Ch3; agreement on skill and economy).

Tagged **Inferred (transcript + slides)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 102). Inference: this criterion adds that position on that spectrum depends on how an exercise is loaded, not only which exercise it is.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The book gives the boxer and shot putter contrast without numbers, so it does not prescribe specific loads. For all-round sports (decathlon, gymnastics, modern pentathlon) the authors say the choice of a main regime is unresolved (see [[claim--all-round-athletes-main-regime-cyclic-and-phasic-tonic]]). Regime matching does not replace the other four criteria.

    13	
    14	# High Jumpers (Nikitin 1983): As Qualification Rises, Isometric Knee-Extension Power Moves Up and Plantarflexor Power Moves Down the Factor Structure
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors present factor analysis as a way to study the structure of special physical preparedness, "especially informative" when it compares athletes of different qualification or one athlete at different stages; data from many sports show "distinct changes in the structure of an athlete's physical preparedness with increasing sports proficiency" (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252). Table 4.1 (Nikitin 1983), "The factor structure (in %) of Special Physical Preparedness of high jumpers, in terms of the major factors displayed by a large sample of competitors of different levels of qualification," verified against the page image:
    17	
    18	| Factor | Class 2-3 athletes | % | Class 1 - MS | % |
    19	|---|---|---|---|---|
    20	| I | General athletic preparedness | 29.6 | Specific athletic preparedness | 27.4 |
    21	| II | Power of plantarflexors | 19.6 | Power of knee extension isometrically | 23.4 |
    22	| III | Power of knee extension in dynamic regime | 13.0 | Power of knee extension dynamically | 18.5 |
    23	| IV | Isometric strength of knee extensors | 10.5 | Power of plantarflexors | 11.8 |
    24	| V | Explosive-strength of knee extensors (isometric) | 6.5 | (none listed) | |
    25	
    26	The authors' reading: higher-class jumpers develop the specific ability to generate powerful take-off force (factor I) and powerful body extension with the knee and back extensors (factor III); explosive force of the take-off leg's extensors under isometric conditions (factor II) "assumes major significance," growing from what were factors IV and V in Class 2-3; plantarflexor indicators move from factor II to factor IV, "the contribution of which diminishes significantly"; and "the role of special physical preparedness of jumpers increases with level of qualification." (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252.)
    27	
    28	**Why it works** — Here the authors do give a mechanism. Isometric strength matters at high level "due to the large loading of the muscles during the take-off, where the support (take-off) leg acts as a lever, and converts into vertical lift the angular velocity acquired during the run-up." Plantarflexors fade "because under intense overloading the muscles of the support leg are already unable to make a significant contribution to the dynamics of the take-off." (PDF p. 263 / printed p. 252.)
    29	
    30	**When to apply** — For jumpers and athletes whose key action is a planted, high-load take-off: as qualification rises, give more weight to isometric and explosive-isometric knee-extensor strength in the take-off position. Inference: the falling plantarflexor share may justify a smaller plantarflexor emphasis, but the book reports a factor share, not a training reduction. More generally, the authors' rule is to plan from "the general trends of change in the factor structure ... with increase in proficiency, as well as the individual peculiarities of a specific athlete" (PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253). Eric's baseline: isometric mid-thigh pull peak force enters the DSI used to choose between plyometric and max-strength emphasis. **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 76). Inference: these data are a reason to keep an isometric knee-extension measure for jumpers, but they say nothing about the DSI ratio itself.
    31	
    32	**When NOT to apply** — The sample is described only as "a large sample"; the number, factor-extraction method and test battery are not given. The percentages do not sum to 100 (about 79% for Class 2-3 and 81% for Class 1-MS), and the text does not say what the remainder is. The labels changing between columns ("general" to "specific" athletic preparedness) mean factors are not the same variables across groups, so the shifts are interpretive. This is high-jump data; Inference: transfer to other take-off actions (a cut, a block) is not shown.
    33	
    34	**Example** — The book's own: Table 4.1 above.
    35

    13	
    14	# Skaters (Shchirkovyets and Rosovtsyev 1977): Aerobic Factors Dominate at Class 1, Energetic Efficiency and Technique Dominate at Master of Sport
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Table 4.2 (Shchirkovyets & Rosovtsyev 1977), "The factor structure (in %) of special fitness of skaters in terms of the major factors displayed by a large sample of competitors of different levels of qualification," verified against the page image (PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253):
    17	
    18	| Factor | Class 1 athletes | % | Master of Sport | % |
    19	|---|---|---|---|---|
    20	| I | Aerobic power | 35.9 | Energetic efficiency of executing specific work | 36.5 |
    21	| II | Aerobic capacity | 23.3 | Multi-faceted technical preparedness | 21.9 |
    22	| III | Power of anaerobic processes | 16.8 | Power of anaerobic processes | 19.8 |
    23	| IV | Energetic efficiency of executing specific work | 2.7 | Aerobic efficiency | 10.9 |
    24	| V | Multi-faceted technical preparedness | 8.9 | (none listed) | |
    25	
    26	The authors note "the sharp rise in the role of energetic efficiency of special work and multifaceted technical preparedness"; that Class 1's first two factors "may be combined as one factor (i.e. aerobic efficiency) whose role at Master of Sport level decreases"; and that "the significance of anaerobic power increases slightly (factor III)" (PDF pp. 263-264 / printed pp. 252-253). Their conclusion: "a high level of aerobic potential still does not ensure top-level performance in skating. To efficiently generate a high level of aerobic power, it [is] necessary to have excellent movement technique and a high level of anaerobic (non-oxidative glycolytic) productivity." Factor research gives "a useful statistical model" of special physical preparedness, whose form depends on the individual's motor qualities and the organisation of training, so programming must consider general trends with rising proficiency, individual peculiarities and changes in the main functional characteristics (PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253).
    27	
    28	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism beyond the statement that technique and anaerobic productivity are needed to use aerobic power efficiently.
    29	
    30	**When to apply** — When an athlete's aerobic markers are already high but performance stalls: shift emphasis toward economy of the specific work, technical preparedness and anaerobic power, as the Master of Sport structure suggests. Eric's baseline: "Movement efficiency (skill) is treated as directly reducing energy cost." Tagged **Inferred (transcript)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 172). Inference: the rise of "energetic efficiency of executing specific work" to the first factor at Master of Sport level (36.5%) is consistent with that teaching point; the Class 1 value for the same factor (2.7) is unclear, so the size of the change should not be quoted.
    31	
    32	**When NOT to apply** — The sample is "a large sample" with no number, method or test battery given. The columns do not sum to 100 (about 88% and 89%), and the remainder is not explained. Factor labels differ between columns, so the comparison is interpretive. Class 1 factor IV (2.7) is smaller than factor V (8.9), against the order of factors by share (verified against the page image, PDF p. 264 / printed p. 253). Inference: 2.7 may be a misprint (12.7 would restore the order and bring the column to about 98%: 35.9 + 23.3 + 16.8 + 12.7 + 8.9 = 97.6), but the source gives no correction, so treat the 2.7 value as unclear. The conclusion that a "high level of anaerobic (non-oxidative glycolytic) productivity" is necessary conflicts with the authors' earlier advice in 4.4 to "decrease the proportion of glycolysis" (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249); see [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]].
    33	
    34	**Example** — The book's own: Table 4.2 above.

In those cases where the working effort is displayed over a brief time interval, a necessary condition of the 
movement’s effectiveness is the speed with which maximum effort is developed. In other words, if it is necessary 
for the athlete to produce a large force within some time limit, he must do it quickly and use a high RFD. Such a 
necessity is dictated by the conditions of the activity and by the biomechanical characteristics of the 
musculoskeletal system, especially the working amplitude of the movement.
Thus, the RFD, or rate with which the required maximum force is developed (determined from the slope of 
the force-time curve), is an important criterion of correspondence for resolving the task of special strength training 
(sec 2.2.1), which relates directly to the characteristics of the neuromuscular system. This again emphasizes the 
fact that all training is primarily neuromuscular and that training based entirely on variables such as exercise 
choice, load, sets and repetitions is highly inadequate for producing sport specific fitness.
It should be stressed that fulfillment of the criterion of correspondence regarding strength and the speed with 
which it achieves a maximum creates its own unique problem, the successful resolution of which depends upon 
the efficiency of the neuromuscular training process.
4.3.5 The Regim e of Muscular Work
The criterion of correspondence regarding the sports regime relies on determining the character of the muscular 
work involved. In particular, the regime of muscular work should be taken into consideration for selecting the 
means and methods of special strength training. 
The fact is that, depending upon the character of its execution, 
the same means can solve different tasks. For example, boxers and shot putters need to execute the same exercise 
(e.g. performing a thrusting arm movement against the resistance of a pulley machine) with different weights, 
tempos, number of sets and repetitions, because boxing requires primarily a quick, unresisted movement and the 
ability to repeat it many times without significant decrease in force, whereas shotputting involves rapid single 
movements against a specific resistance.
The selection of a regime of muscular work is difficult where a specific motor action is concerned. However, 
it is even more difficult in all-round sports like decathlon, gymnastics and modem pentathlon. Therefore, the 
problem of selecting a regime of muscular work involves two obvious tasks:
• selection of the regime for a specific motor action (e.g. the key elements in an exercise)
• selection of the main regime which will best develop all of the diverse muscular activities in all-round training.
The latter issue is still far from being resolved, although the evolution of training methods in sport indicates that it 
should be more thoroughly understood in the near future.
Almost one hundred years of experience in training all-round track athletes indicates that their fundamental 
training regime is speed-cyclic with dynamic tension, primarily of the explosive type. This was corroborated by 
using statistical analysis to identify the key exercises in the 'all-round' complex (Zatsiorsky, 1966; Lukauskas, 
1967; Mamdzhanyan, 1976). To corroborate this idea one should examine the preparation of gymnasts. For a long 
time they adhered to primarily static training, with many of them including some dynamic exercises such as 
jumping. The progress of competitive standards and the necessity to master complex elements such as jumping 
with extensive longitudinal rotation compelled them to examine the value of the cyclic work regime and reconsider 
it in favour of dynamic muscular tension.
Thus, it may be concluded that cyclic and phasic-tonic regimes probably should be regarded as the most 
important in all-round training. It is also necessary to add other regimes, determined by the motor skills required 
by the specific sport. However, this conclusion needs rigorous experimental substantiation.
In conjunction with perfecting motor skills in a specific activity, one should consider the importance of 
changing from one activity to another in those exercises where this is necessary. Thus, an athlete's results in the 
long jump are determined mainly by the ability to switch from the cyclic regime of muscular work in running, to 
explosive effort in the take-off. For instance, good gymnasts are capable of switching rapidly from dynamic 
explosive effort to isometric tension. The methodology underlying the development of these complex capabilities 
is the aim of technical training in all sport. Its resolution is the goal of special strength training.

=================== heuristic--rfd-as-correspondence-criterion-and-impulse-cannot-compare-movements.md
# Use the Rate of Force Development as a Correspondence Criterion; Do Not Use Impulse to Compare Different Movements

**What it is** — The criterion of correspondence for "the rate of developing maximum force" complements the dynamic-effort criterion and "is particularly important in those sporting activities requiring explosive strength" (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246). "The ability to increase power or explosive strength also depends on specifically training the RFD factor," which the authors call "vital" to programme design for any sport with explosive actions, and they name plyometric training as "one of the practical consequences" of this analysis. Explosive strength may be evaluated by power, impulse (F.Δt) or the Reactivity Coefficient (RC = Fmax/tmax.mg = RFDmax/W), "although the significance of each of them can be different": impulse "is acceptable only when it is not necessary to compare different movements"; comparing movements would be valid "only if the time taken is identical for each movement, a situation that does not occur in human movement," so for that purpose "determination of the impulse of the force is irrelevant" (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246). Where effort lasts only briefly, "if it is necessary for the athlete to produce a large force within some time limit, he must do it quickly and use a high RFD," a necessity set by the activity and "especially the working amplitude of the movement." RFD "is an important criterion of correspondence ... which relates directly to the characteristics of the neuromuscular system," and "all training is primarily neuromuscular and ... training based entirely on variables such as exercise choice, load, sets and repetitions is highly inadequate for producing sport specific fitness" (PDF p. 258 / printed p. 247).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning: when the time available is limited by the movement's amplitude, how fast force rises decides how much force can be applied; and impulse depends on duration, so two movements of different duration cannot be compared on it. They tie RFD to "the characteristics of the neuromuscular system" without further mechanism here.

**When to apply** — When an action has a short force-application window (jumps, sprints, throws, blocking contact): pick exercises and tests that reproduce the rate of force rise, not just peak force; use RFD or RC rather than impulse when comparing different exercises or tests. Eric's baseline: mRSI from daily CMJ testing is the daily readiness marker [**Explicit**, `docs/method-baseline.md`, line 74], and the CMJ family is run on ForceDecks [**Inferred (protocol; author uncertain)**, line 77]. Inference: mRSI is a time-normalised jump index, so it fits this criterion's preference for rate over impulse; the book does not discuss mRSI.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors' rejection of impulse is scoped to comparing different movements; they accept it within one movement. Their statement that training built only on exercise choice, load, sets and repetitions is "highly inadequate" is a strong judgment without cited data. The RC formula repeats the 2.2.1 definition; the book defines RC in more than one way elsewhere (see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]), so check which form a source means.

**Example** — The book's own: plyometric training as the practical consequence of treating RFD as a trainable factor (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246).

**Related** — [[claim--average-or-peak-force-times-velocity-is-not-power]], [[principle--training-effort-must-match-or-exceed-sport-effort-judged-by-movement-speed]], [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]], [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]], [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]], [[science-and-practice-of-strength-training--zatsiorsky/framework--explosive-strength-deficit-and-rate-of-force-development-indices]].
=================== principle--training-effort-must-match-or-exceed-sport-effort-judged-by-movement-speed.md
# Training Effort Should Not Fall Below the Sport's Effort, and Movement Speed Decides Which Kind of Maximal Effort Counts

**What it is** — The criterion of dynamic effort is "the quantitative correspondence of the dynamics of the training means to the specific sports movement": "the intensity of the training stimulus should not be less than that encountered in the given exercise at the corresponding level of sports proficiency and should even exceed it" (PDF p. 256 / printed p. 245). The authors then ask "whether the maximum value or the mean value should be considered as the criterion of correspondence of strength." Maximal strength shows in two forms, moving heavy loads or light loads, and peak force can be larger with the light load "since the lighter load can be rapidly accelerated (remembering that F = ma)." Yet "it is unnecessary to exercise only with light loads, even if the maximum achieved corresponds closely to the dynamics of the special exercise," because the two forces are "qualitatively different: in the first, maximum force is determined by the absolute strength of the muscles, and in the second by the speed of contraction," so their training effects differ too. The athlete should know the type of strength needed and match "the amount of effort and the movement time"; "correspondence with respect to the maximum and mean magnitude of strength can be determined only by calculating the speed of movement" (PDF p. 256 / printed p. 245). Their two examples: a special exercise against "a large resistance at a relatively low speed" calls for training "aimed primarily at developing maximal strength"; one with "a small resistance" at maximal speed calls for "a moderate amount of effort" with "particular attention to the duration of the movement" (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246).

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanical reason (F = ma: a light load accelerated hard can produce a high peak force) and a qualitative one (heavy-load force is limited by absolute strength, light-load force by contraction speed). They give no physiological detail beyond that here.

**When to apply** — When setting loads for a special strength exercise: first estimate the sport action's resistance and speed (or movement time), then pick heavy, slow loading for high-resistance, low-speed actions and moderate, fast loading with attention to movement time for low-resistance, high-speed actions. Eric's baseline: "Training time is deliberately weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints)." Tagged **Inferred (transcript + slides)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 104). Eric's baseline: the dynamic strength index (CMJ against IMTP) is used "to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 76), tagged in the baseline as [contested] by the evidence check. Inference: the DSI decision is an athlete-side version of this criterion's task-side question (is the limiting force set by absolute strength or by speed of contraction).

**When NOT to apply** — An ambiguity in the text: the criterion says training effort "should not be less than" the sport's and "should even exceed it," while the light-fast example prescribes "a moderate amount of effort" (PDF pp. 256-257 / printed pp. 245-246). Inference: the two fit if "effort" means force magnitude relative to the sport's own (moderate in a light, fast sport), but the authors do not say so. The text gives no method for "calculating the speed of movement" or a threshold that separates the two cases, so the rule is qualitative.

**Example** — The book's own pair: overcoming a large resistance at low speed (train maximal strength) against moving a small resistance at maximal speed (moderate effort, attention to movement duration) (PDF p. 257 / printed p. 246).

**Related** — [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[principle--force-time-profile-determines-strength-vs-power-training-target]] (Ch2, the same choice argued from the force-time curve; agreement), [[framework--two-force-regimes-overcoming-weight-vs-inertia]] (4.2.2), [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]], [[heuristic--rfd-as-correspondence-criterion-and-impulse-cannot-compare-movements]] (4.3.4, which the authors say complements this criterion).
=================== claim--local-blood-flow-not-vo2max-tracks-competition-period-endurance-gains.md
# In the Competition Period, Local Blood Flow to the Working Muscles Rises While VO2 Max Falls, and the Authors Credit Endurance Gains to the Blood Flow

**What it is** — "Recently, haemodynamic factors have been shown to play an important role in the functional specialisation of the body during endurance work" (nine citations). In italics: "The redistribution of blood and an increase in circulation to the working muscles contributes to satisfying the oxygen requirements of the muscles and the removal of anaerobic metabolites." This "Differentiation of the vesicular reaction providing effective redistribution of blood flow" (Inference: "vesicular" is probably meant as "vascular") develops in the competition period "as a result of the extensive aerobic loading executed during the preparatory period." In 25 km road cycling, improved performance came with a fall in VO2 max in the competition period while "peak blood flow to the lower extremities increases," and cardiac output also fell (Stepochkin et al 1970). (PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249, verified against the page image.) "OBLA (lactate threshold) and VO2 max levels can change independently": while VO2 max falls somewhat in the competition period, "OBLA can rise" (Zatsiorsky et al 1974; Sirenko 1979; Nurmekivan 1974). In qualified skaters the mean change in VO2 max in the competition period is "5-10%," while local blood flow rises "much more significantly (50-250%)" (Mellenberg 1981). The authors conclude that training effectiveness "does not lie in raising VO2 max, but in enhancing the haemodynamic efficiency of oxygen transport," and that, with the muscles' strength and oxidative qualities, "the redistribution of bloodflow and improved local vesicular reaction are important conditions for developing local muscle endurance." (PDF p. 261 / printed p. 250, verified against the page image.) Because these conditions lessen dependence on VO2 max, the assumed "antagonism in endurance sport between the development of the aerobic and anaerobic mechanisms must be questioned (Mellenberg & Khvan, 1982)" (PDF pp. 260-261 / printed pp. 249-250).

**Why it works** — The authors' mechanism: more blood to the working muscles meets their oxygen need and clears anaerobic metabolites, so less glycolysis is needed, which also explains why VO2 max can fall without harm. They support it by citation; the text gives no figures beyond those above.

**When to apply** — When interpreting in-season test results: a flat or falling VO2 max during the competition period need not mean lost endurance if threshold measures and performance hold. Build the aerobic base in the preparatory period, since the authors credit the competition-period blood-flow change to that loading. Eric's baseline: "For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery ... not distance capacity." Tagged **Inferred (transcript)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 123). Inference: local blood-flow capacity is a plausible route for that recovery, but the book discusses endurance athletes, not repeat-sprint sports.

**When NOT to apply** — A sentence on the same page is unclear: "blood lactate concentration can increase by some 6% as a result of training, while the VO2 max level increases by only 7% (Williams et al, 1967)" (PDF p. 261 / printed p. 250; the image confirms 6% and 7%). As printed, 7% is larger than 6%, so "only" does not fit; the intended figure or measure (perhaps the lactate threshold rather than lactate concentration) cannot be recovered from the text. Do not cite it. The 50-250% blood-flow range is wide and given without method. The antagonism point is the authors developing an argument across two pages (offered as a possible explanation on p.249, questioned on p.250), not settled.

**Example** — The book's own: 25 km road cyclists whose performance improved while VO2 max and cardiac output fell and leg blood flow rose (Stepochkin et al 1970; PDF p. 260 / printed p. 249).

**Related** — [[claim--vo2max-alone-does-not-determine-endurance-performance]], [[claim--endurance-rests-on-muscle-oxidative-and-strength-qualities-not-vo2max]], [[principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles]], [[framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]].

SUPERTRAINING
coefficient is R = 0.7 during the preparation period, whereas it is 0.4 during the competitive period (Vasiliev 
& Trunin, 1974; Melenberg, 1981).
This data indicates that V02 max on its own is no guarantee of outstanding performance. It is now recognised 
that, apart from aerobic power, other factors play a role, such as the ability to perform work for a prolonged 
period at a level of oxygen consumption close to the V02 max, and the ability to effectively utilise available 
energy under competitive conditions. This concerns the decrease in V02 max during the competition period, a 
phenomenon possibly explained by the decreasing trainability of aerobic processes or by an inherent antagonism 
between aerobic and anaerobic processes (Zatsiorsky et al, 1974; Volkov, 1975).
Oxidative Capacity and Muscular Endurance
Practical improvement of the metabolic processes in endurance sports is associated with increasing the potential 
to utilise aerobic sources of energy by raising the Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation (OBLA), i.e. that level of 
oxygen consumption at which the anaerobic processes begin to be prominently activated. Anaerobic work is 
approximately 50% more effective than aerobic work in raising this lactate threshold, therefore it is to the athlete's 
advantage to execute prolonged, intense work without the preliminary accumulation of lactate and include 
maerobic energy production (Christensen & Hogberg, 1950).
Since OBLA depends on V02 max, it is considered useful to strive to raise VO2 max, and in particular, to 
create some reserve of aerobic power by the end o f the preparatory period to avoid a decrease in V02 max during 
the competition period, which may lower the specific work-capacity. Considering that a significant amount of the 
energy production of intense muscular work is achieved by recruiting the glycolytic mechanism of ATP 
resynthesis, it is advisable to execute a specific part of the training load with a high blood lactate concentration.
However, recent research indicates that an increase in endurance is associated more with enhancing the
