=================== claim--400m-stride-length-held-by-local-strength-endurance.md
# Faster 400 m Runners Hold Stride Length Through Local Strength-Endurance; Under Fatigue, Stride Length Falls More Than Tempo

**What it is** — The authors illustrate local muscular endurance with the 400 m: "It is clear that stride length is maintained with some decrease in tempo at the high-mastery level by means of local strength-endurance. In the fatigued state, athletes of different sex and level of qualification all display a greater decrease in stride length than tempo, but the decrease in speed is associated exclusively with the strength factor." (PDF p. 261 / printed p. 250.) Fig 4.23 (Popov 1972), "Change in stride length accompanying increase in the speed of running 400m," verified against the page image: the x-axis is 400 m time from 53 s to 46 s (faster to the right); the left axes give stride length (200-230 cm) and stride rate (3.7-3.9 per second), the right axis number of strides (170-200). The stride-length line rises from about 207 cm at 53 s to about 227 cm at 46 s, slowly at first and steeply from about 48 s. A line labelled stride rate rises to a peak near 50 s and then declines toward 46 s. The label placement makes the number-of-strides line hard to tell apart from the stride-rate line, so no values are read for those two.

**Why it works** — The authors attribute the held stride length to local strength-endurance and the loss of speed under fatigue "exclusively" to the strength factor; they give no further mechanism or data beyond the figure.

**When to apply** — For 400 m and similar speed-endurance events: treat the ability to keep stride length late in the race as a strength-endurance target, and use special strength exercises in the event's regime to build it (the authors' general prescription for local endurance, same page). Eric's baseline: "Speed is taught as the quality with the shortest ground-contact-time demand." Tagged **Inferred (transcript)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 96). Inference: for football, repeated sprints over a drive are much shorter than 400 m, so this claim fits defensive backs' or receivers' long-run fatigue only loosely.

**When NOT to apply** — "Exclusively with the strength factor" is a strong statement resting on one cited data set (Popov 1972) whose athletes, sample and method are not described. The figure's x-axis is 400 m race time, not time within a race. Inference: it therefore plots runners (or performances) of different speeds, not fatigue within one race, so it does not itself show the fatigue claim; the caption does not say whether the data are cross-sectional or longitudinal. Inference: stride rate also declines at the fastest times in the figure, so the figure alone does not rule out a frequency contribution.

**Example** — The book's own: Fig 4.23, where faster 400 m times come with longer strides and, at the fastest times, a slight fall in stride rate (Popov 1972; PDF p. 261 / printed p. 250).

**Related** — [[principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles]], [[framework--strength-endurance-taxonomy-and-absolute-vs-partial]], [[claim--three-zone-force-velocity-curve-for-cyclic-locomotion]].
=================== framework--four-level-functional-specialisation-and-special-physical-preparedness.md
# Functional Specialisation in Four Levels: General Abilities, Coordination, Explosive Force and Specific Endurance, Then the Structure of Special Physical Preparedness

**What it is** — Under "The Process of Functional Specialisation," the authors give "an ascending flowchart" of how the body specialises "over many years of training" (Fig 4.24, verified against the page image; PDF p. 262 / printed p. 251):
- **Level 1 (generalised abilities):** speed, strength and endurance, the "flexible mechanisms of coordination, regulation and energy production" that serve daily life and "offer extensive possibilities for adaptation."
- **Level 2:** coordination. The demands of sport "stimulate the motor function, which coordinates all muscular activity."
- **Level 3:** the ability to display explosive force, and specific endurance. "The motor function specialises chiefly by developing the ability to display explosive force and specific endurance independent of the type of sport." Specific endurance "may be predominantly cardiovascular or local muscular in nature," and explosive force relates to starting strength, acceleration-strength and absolute strength (3.2.1).
- **Level 4 (specialised abilities):** the structure of special physical preparedness, formed in "the intensive stage of functional specialisation," which "displays its own form with respect to interaction of the cardiovascular-respiratory and motor systems."

Within these structures the functional systems relate by **cooperation** ("effective interaction of all the systems") or **subordination** ("the productivity of one system is enhanced by the functional potentials of the others"). "The structure of special physical preparedness is determined by the specific training regime, and does not relate to conditions imposed by other sporting activities. This fact should be noted by anyone who may be contemplating the use of generalised cross training with various sports." (PDF pp. 262-263 / printed pp. 251-252, verified against the page images.)

**Why it works** — The authors present it as a description of the general sequence, not a tested model; the only mechanism given is that sporting demands stimulate the motor function, which then specialises. No data are attached to the flowchart.

**When to apply** — As a long-term development map: build general speed, strength and endurance and coordination first, then explosive force and specific endurance, then the sport's own structure of preparedness. Use the cross-training warning when another sport is proposed as preparation: the authors say it does not build the target sport's special preparedness. Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next)" is the department's programming "compass." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 101). Inference: both are bottom-up hierarchies that end in sport-specific ability; the Vermeil sequence orders physical qualities, while this flowchart puts coordination below explosive force and specific endurance.

**When NOT to apply** — "Independent of the type of sport" at Level 3 and "does not relate to conditions imposed by other sporting activities" at Level 4 pull in different directions: Level 3 is general across sports, Level 4 is not. The text gives no ages, durations or criteria for moving between levels. The cross-training statement is a strong claim without cited data; it addresses special preparedness, not general fitness or recovery uses of other sports.

**Example** — The book gives no worked example for the flowchart; its factor-analysis tables for high jumpers and skaters (see Related) are offered as data on the Level 4 structure.

**Related** — [[case-study--high-jumper-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[case-study--skater-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[framework--key-specific-nonspecific-levelling-motor-ability-model]] (Ch2.3.4), [[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]] (Ch2.3.1; agreement), [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]] (Ch3.2.1), [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]] (Ch1.5).
=================== heuristic--match-amplitude-direction-and-line-of-resistance-to-the-sport.md
# Match the Exercise's Range, Force Direction and Line of Resistance to the Sport, Not Just the Muscles

**What it is** — The first correspondence criterion, amplitude and direction of movement, "determines which muscles are involved in the work and allows for anatomical peculiarities and the external conditions of work" (PDF p. 253 / printed p. 242). The authors give four illustrations:
- A rower's and a shot putter's shoulder movements have about the same amplitude, but the force direction differs: the oar pull is shoulder extension, the put is shoulder flexion against the shot's inertia (Fig 4.17, verified against the page image).
- Sprinters and jumpers who train hip flexors standing on a hip-flexor machine (pad against the front of the thigh) do not reproduce the sport, because thigh amplitude in running and jumping is "significantly greater" and "begins at an angle of about 210° in the hip joint, relative to the torso." Changing the athlete's position (Fig 4.18, verified against the page image: the athlete lies back on an inclined bench with the working leg swinging up through an arc from below the line of the board) meets the criterion because the resistance "imitates the inertial resistance of the mass of the leg rotating about the hip joint." Load, repetitions and tempo then set whether force or strength-endurance is developed.
- A knapsack of sand or a weight belt, used in middle-distance running, skiing and skating, loads "the muscles which bear the load are those which resist the weight of the body": it can raise tolerance of vertical loading and general strength-endurance "but does not strengthen those muscles which propel the body horizontally."
- A skater's one-leg jumps on the floor or from a bench strengthen the supporting leg and back static-endurance but do not reproduce the push-off, "where the force is directed backward"; skaters should change the direction of resistance instead (Fig 4.19, Verkhoshansky 1977, verified against the page image: a partner-held tether, a weighted sled, and a partner seated on a sled, each pulled in a skating posture). (PDF pp. 253-254 / printed pp. 242-243.)

The rule the authors draw: "select the exact starting position and posture of the athlete, as well as to calculate the direction of action of the forces associated with the working links of the system and the additional load," and take into account "the line of action of the applied external resistance" (PDF p. 253 / printed p. 242).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is mechanical: the muscles that work are the ones that oppose the resistance along its line of action, so a load acting vertically trains anti-gravity muscles, not horizontal propulsors, and a range that starts at the wrong hip angle trains the wrong part of the movement. They give no further physiological mechanism.

**When to apply** — When choosing resisted drills or special strength exercises: trace the line of action of the resistance and the joint range it loads, and compare both with the sport action. Use it to screen weighted vests, belts and limb loads before calling them "speed" work. Eric's baseline: Dynamic Correspondence, "matching amplitude/direction of movement ... to the sport skill, governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 103). Inference: a sled or partner-resisted start loads horizontally, which by this criterion fits acceleration better than a vertical vest load; the book does not discuss sleds for sprinters here.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors do not dismiss vertical loading: they say it can still build tolerance of vertical loading and general strength-endurance, so a vest or belt has a general role even though it fails this criterion for horizontal propulsion. The 210° hip figure is given without a source or measurement method and should not be read as a measured norm. Matching range and direction is one of five criteria; it does not settle load, speed or regime (see [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]]).

**Example** — The book's own: the standing hip-flexor machine against the inclined-bench hip-flexion exercise of Fig 4.18, for sprinters and jumpers (PDF p. 253 / printed p. 242).

**Related** — [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[heuristic--train-force-at-the-accentuated-joint-angle]] (4.3.2 continues the same hip-flexor example), [[claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output]] (Ch3, the sartorius correlation at 210° hip angle), [[framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines]] (4.2.7, the machine-design side of the same problem), [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--wearable-resistance-kinetic-energy-sprint]].

- **Level 4 (specialised abilities):** the structure of special physical preparedness, formed in "the intensive stage of functional specialisation," which "displays its own form with respect to interaction of the cardiovascular-respiratory and motor systems."

Within these structures the functional systems relate by **cooperation** ("effective interaction of all the systems") or **subordination** ("the productivity of one system is enhanced by the functional potentials of the others"). "The structure of special physical preparedness is determined by the specific training regime, and does not relate to conditions imposed by other sporting activities. This fact should be noted by anyone who may be contemplating the use of generalised cross training with various sports." (PDF pp. 262-263 / printed pp. 251-252, verified against the page images.)

**Why it works** — The authors present it as a description of the general sequence, not a tested model; the only mechanism given is that sporting demands stimulate the motor function, which then specialises. No data are attached to the flowchart.

**When to apply** — As a long-term development map: build general speed, strength and endurance and coordination first, then explosive force and specific endurance, then the sport's own structure of preparedness. Use the cross-training warning when another sport is proposed as preparation: the authors say it does not build the target sport's special preparedness. Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next)" is the department's programming "compass." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 101). Inference: both are bottom-up hierarchies that end in sport-specific ability; the Vermeil sequence orders physical qualities, while this flowchart puts coordination below explosive force and specific endurance.

**When NOT to apply** — "Independent of the type of sport" at Level 3 and "does not relate to conditions imposed by other sporting activities" at Level 4 pull in different directions: Level 3 is general across sports, Level 4 is not. The text gives no ages, durations or criteria for moving between levels. The cross-training statement is a strong claim without cited data; it addresses special preparedness, not general fitness or recovery uses of other sports.

**Example** — The book gives no worked example for the flowchart; its factor-analysis tables for high jumpers and skaters (see Related) are offered as data on the Level 4 structure.

**Related** — [[case-study--high-jumper-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[case-study--skater-factor-structure-by-qualification]], [[principle--motor-system-leads-cardiorespiratory-adaptation-do-not-separate-them]], [[framework--key-specific-nonspecific-levelling-motor-ability-model]] (Ch2.3.4), [[claim--physical-quality-transfer-decreases-as-specific-fitness-increases]] (Ch2.3.1; agreement), [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]] (Ch3.2.1), [[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]] (Ch1.5).
=================== heuristic--match-amplitude-direction-and-line-of-resistance-to-the-sport.md
# Match the Exercise's Range, Force Direction and Line of Resistance to the Sport, Not Just the Muscles

**What it is** — The first correspondence criterion, amplitude and direction of movement, "determines which muscles are involved in the work and allows for anatomical peculiarities and the external conditions of work" (PDF p. 253 / printed p. 242). The authors give four illustrations:
- A rower's and a shot putter's shoulder movements have about the same amplitude, but the force direction differs: the oar pull is shoulder extension, the put is shoulder flexion against the shot's inertia (Fig 4.17, verified against the page image).
- Sprinters and jumpers who train hip flexors standing on a hip-flexor machine (pad against the front of the thigh) do not reproduce the sport, because thigh amplitude in running and jumping is "significantly greater" and "begins at an angle of about 210° in the hip joint, relative to the torso." Changing the athlete's position (Fig 4.18, verified against the page image: the athlete lies back on an inclined bench with the working leg swinging up through an arc from below the line of the board) meets the criterion because the resistance "imitates the inertial resistance of the mass of the leg rotating about the hip joint." Load, repetitions and tempo then set whether force or strength-endurance is developed.
- A knapsack of sand or a weight belt, used in middle-distance running, skiing and skating, loads "the muscles which bear the load are those which resist the weight of the body": it can raise tolerance of vertical loading and general strength-endurance "but does not strengthen those muscles which propel the body horizontally."
- A skater's one-leg jumps on the floor or from a bench strengthen the supporting leg and back static-endurance but do not reproduce the push-off, "where the force is directed backward"; skaters should change the direction of resistance instead (Fig 4.19, Verkhoshansky 1977, verified against the page image: a partner-held tether, a weighted sled, and a partner seated on a sled, each pulled in a skating posture). (PDF pp. 253-254 / printed pp. 242-243.)

The rule the authors draw: "select the exact starting position and posture of the athlete, as well as to calculate the direction of action of the forces associated with the working links of the system and the additional load," and take into account "the line of action of the applied external resistance" (PDF p. 253 / printed p. 242).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is mechanical: the muscles that work are the ones that oppose the resistance along its line of action, so a load acting vertically trains anti-gravity muscles, not horizontal propulsors, and a range that starts at the wrong hip angle trains the wrong part of the movement. They give no further physiological mechanism.

**When to apply** — When choosing resisted drills or special strength exercises: trace the line of action of the resistance and the joint range it loads, and compare both with the sport action. Use it to screen weighted vests, belts and limb loads before calling them "speed" work. Eric's baseline: Dynamic Correspondence, "matching amplitude/direction of movement ... to the sport skill, governs whether an exercise actually transfers, rather than surface resemblance to the sport." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)** (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 103). Inference: a sled or partner-resisted start loads horizontally, which by this criterion fits acceleration better than a vertical vest load; the book does not discuss sleds for sprinters here.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors do not dismiss vertical loading: they say it can still build tolerance of vertical loading and general strength-endurance, so a vest or belt has a general role even though it fails this criterion for horizontal propulsion. The 210° hip figure is given without a source or measurement method and should not be read as a measured norm. Matching range and direction is one of five criteria; it does not settle load, speed or regime (see [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]]).

**Example** — The book's own: the standing hip-flexor machine against the inclined-bench hip-flexion exercise of Fig 4.18, for sprinters and jumpers (PDF p. 253 / printed p. 242).

**Related** — [[framework--five-criteria-of-dynamic-correspondence]], [[heuristic--train-force-at-the-accentuated-joint-angle]] (4.3.2 continues the same hip-flexor example), [[claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output]] (Ch3, the sartorius correlation at 210° hip angle), [[framework--functional-vs-nonfunctional-resistance-machines]] (4.2.7, the machine-design side of the same problem), [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--wearable-resistance-kinetic-energy-sprint]].

**What I found:**
- **Power entry** (`claim--average-or-peak-force-times-velocity-is-not-power`): the physics is now right.
  - It says instantaneous P = F·v holds for any force.
  - It says constant force matters only when one force value stands for a whole interval.
  - It says the real error is multiplying an average or peak force by an average or peak velocity.
  - `proven` covers only the identity P = dW/dt = F·v; the authors' constant-force condition and their practical advice are explicitly left out of it.
  - I checked the equations and both source oddities against the page image (PDF 257).
- **Fixer disagreements:** all five are justified.
  1. Their objection to the review's "only" is correct physics: average power also equals average force times velocity when velocity is constant.
  2. Quoting all three Fig 4.22 sentences is supported by PDF 256.
  3. Labelling the skater misprint guess as "Inference:" follows the standards.
  4. The extra "Naturally, running speed determines..." quote is exact on PDF 255.
  5. Skipping a separate OBLA entry is fine; I confirmed those quotes already sit in the two endurance entries.
- **The other seven fixes:** each round-1 problem is gone. Every new quote matches the page, and both factor tables match their page images (PDF 263-264). The skater table still shows the printed 2.7, now flagged as unclear.
- **`_book.md`:** the Chapter 4 row reads "done | 64". The files on disk agree (6 + 35 + 13 + 10). The 4.3 row (13) and 4.4 row (10) match, and the stale sentence is gone.
- **Links:** all 125 wikilinks in the 23 files resolve. The old power-entry slug appears nowhere in staging entries or the vault, only in the round-1 review and the fix log, which are historical records.
